core: Mesopotamia ('land between the rivers') lay in the Fertile Crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates, in and around modern Iraq; the rivers' unpredictable flooding required cooperative irrigation, which supported dense farming, food surpluses, and the first cities

Sumer in southern Mesopotamia developed independent city-states — Uruk, Ur, Eridu, Lagash, Nippur — each centered on a temple; Uruk was among the world's earliest large cities, with a population possibly near 50,000 by the end of the 4th millennium BCE

Cuneiform, developed by the Sumerians (proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk c. 3200 BCE; a fuller script by around 3000 BCE), is among the world's earliest writing systems: wedge-shaped signs pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus
Ziggurats were stepped, mud-brick temple-towers at the center of Mesopotamian cities, topped by a shrine to the city's patron deity; large ziggurats were in use by around 2100 BCE
Later empires unified the region: the Akkadian Empire under Sargon of Akkad (reign c. 2334-2279 BCE, 'around 2300 BCE') was the first known empire; Babylon later rose under Hammurabi

The Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), inscribed on a basalt stele in cuneiform Akkadian, is one of the earliest known written law codes: 282 laws, organized as case law, applying lex talionis ('an eye for an eye') with penalties that varied by the social class of victim and offender
Key Mesopotamian contributions: the wheel (c. 3500 BCE), a sexagesimal (base-60) number system that survives in 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles, and systematic astronomy
supporting: Agriculture reached Mesopotamia by around 8000 BCE; by roughly 4500 BCE farming villages were becoming urban centers
Bronze metallurgy developed after around 4000 BCE, alongside the plow and the wheel
The Akkadian Empire ended in the late 3rd millennium BCE (OpenStax gives 2193 BCE; other scholars c. 2154 BCE)
The stele of Hammurabi was excavated at Susa (Iran) in 1901-1902 and is held at the Louvre

claims.claim: Mesopotamia lay in the Fertile Crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (largely modern Iraq); because the rivers flooded erratically and unpredictably, its early inhabitants built cooperative irrigation works, and the resulting farming surpluses supported some of the world's first cities.

Sumer in southern Mesopotamia was organized into independent city-states such as Uruk, Ur, Eridu, Lagash, and Nippur; Uruk was among the earliest large cities, with a population that may have approached 50,000 by the end of the 4th millennium BCE.

The Sumerians developed cuneiform — wedge-shaped signs pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus — one of the world's earliest writing systems; the earliest (proto-cuneiform) tablets from Uruk date to about 3200 BCE, and OpenStax notes a script had developed by around 3000 BCE, if not earlier.
A ziggurat was a stepped, mud-brick temple-tower at the heart of a Mesopotamian city, topped by a shrine to the city's patron god; monumental ziggurats were in use by around 2100 BCE.
Sargon of Akkad (reign c. 2334-2279 BCE, 'around 2300 BCE') founded the Akkadian Empire, the first known empire, uniting the previously independent Sumerian city-states under a single ruler.

The Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), created under King Hammurabi of Babylon and inscribed in cuneiform Akkadian on a black basalt stele, is one of the earliest known written law codes: 282 case-law provisions that apply lex talionis ('an eye for an eye') with punishments that varied according to the social class of those involved.

Mesopotamian contributions include the wheel (c. 3500 BCE) and a sexagesimal (base-60) number system whose legacy survives in the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle, alongside systematic astronomical observation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact date of the Code of Hammurabi and of Hammurabi's reign.
positions: Widely cited scholarship dates the code to c. 1754 BCE and Hammurabi's reign to c. 1792-1750 BCE (middle chronology).
The Louvre dates the code to 'around 1750 BC'; World History Encyclopedia gives 'around 1772 BCE'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the code as c. 1754 BCE (the most commonly cited figure) and states plainly that Bronze Age dates are approximate and vary by chronology, attributing the range; it never presents a single date as exact.

positions: The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are dated to about 3200 BCE.
OpenStax describes a cuneiform script that had developed 'by around 3000 BCE, if not earlier'; World History Encyclopedia dates the invention nearer 3600-3500 BCE.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses c. 3200 BCE for the earliest writing while noting a developed script by around 3000 BCE, and marks all such early dates as approximate.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'Mesopotamia' as a generic, self-referential 'foundational History concept' with a circular vocabulary entry ('A foundational History concept covered in this lesson') and gave no actual historical content — no rivers, cities, writing, empires, or dates.
The draft's toolbox-drawer and map-legend analogies conveyed nothing about Mesopotamia and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a substantive, sourced account of Mesopotamian geography, Sumerian city-states, cuneiform, ziggurats, the Akkadian and Babylonian empires, the Code of Hammurabi, and key contributions.
Gave every date with 'c.' where approximate and attributed contested dates (Hammurabi's code, cuneiform's first appearance) rather than stating a single figure as certain.
Described the Code of Hammurabi factually, including its retributive lex talionis and class-based penalties, without endorsing or condemning it in presentist terms.

sourceRecords.title: Mesopotamia (definition article)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports: Mesopotamia as the land 'between two rivers' (Tigris and Euphrates) in the Fertile Crescent, corresponding to modern Iraq, Syria, Kuwait, and Turkey; Sumerian cities Ur, Uruk, Eridu, Lagash, Nippur, with Uruk understood by modern scholars as among the earliest cities; writing developing independently in several regions; ziggurats in use by approximately 2100 BCE at Eridu, Uruk, Ur, and Nippur; Sargon of Akkad's reign 2334-2279 BCE establishing history's first multinational realm; Hammurabi reigning 1792-1750 BCE and the Code of Hammurabi as 'one of the earliest codes of law in the world'; the number sixty as the basic unit; the wheel c. 3500 BCE. Used to cross-check dates against OpenStax; where the two differ (e.g. cuneiform's earliest date, the Akkadian Empire's end) the lesson reports a range. Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Restrictive reuse terms; facts used, wording original.

sourceRecords.title: The Code of Hammurabi (Département des Antiquités orientales)
sourceRecords.notes: Museum object page for the stele held at the Louvre. Supports: King Hammurabi of Babylon created the legal collection 'around 1750 BC'; the monument is a black basalt stele over 2.25 m tall inscribed in cuneiform; it is a 'sweeping collection of jurisprudence' of 282 legal judgements; Law 196 — 'If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out' — illustrating lex talionis, which the Louvre frames as requiring punishment 'proportional to the damages suffered'; discovered 1902 at Susa (Iran). The class-based character of penalties is drawn from OpenStax and World History Encyclopedia, not the Louvre. Fetched via WebFetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-19. Copyrighted museum text; facts used, wording original apart from the short attributed Law 196 quotation (a translation of a public-domain ancient legal text).
